intro: Optimizing building energy usage on your Mac requires moving from reactive spreadsheet management to proactive data analysis. Facilities managers often struggle with energy data because it exists in disconnected silos, making it hard to find real savings.

blocks.text: The challenge of energy data analysis

Facilities managers face a persistent problem with energy data analysis. You likely receive utility bills from different providers, each with its own format. Then you have building management system logs, sub-meter readings, and occupancy data. These sources rarely talk to each other. You end up spending hours manually copying numbers into Excel just to see the big picture.

This manual consolidation is the core of the problem. When you spend your time typing numbers, you lose the chance to analyze them. You might miss that a HVAC unit is running all weekend because you are too busy fixing the formatting in your spreadsheet. This is where the 2 to 4 percent data gap comes from. You have the data, but you cannot use it efficiently.

items: Data silos: Systems for lighting, HVAC, and water do not share a common database.
Manual entry: Typing data from PDF bills into spreadsheets leads to errors and delays.
Lack of context: Raw numbers do not tell you if the building was actually occupied that day.
Operational priority: Energy management is often treated as a secondary task instead of a daily focus.

blocks.text: You do not need an expensive overhaul to start seeing improvements. Start by automating your data collection. If you use Microsoft 365, use Power Query in Excel to pull data directly from CSV files provided by your utility companies. This removes the need for manual typing.

Next, focus on granularity. Monthly bills hide waste. If you can, set up sub-metering for major equipment. Even simple smart plugs on smaller devices can show you what is drawing power when it should be off. Compare these readings against your building's occupancy schedule.
Using your Mac for energy analytics

Your Mac is a powerful tool for this work. Use Safari or Chrome to access cloud-based platforms like EnergyCAP or MRI Energy. These tools are built for the web, so they run perfectly on macOS. Use the built-in Screen Capture tool by pressing ⌘ ⇧ 4 to grab charts for your reports. You can then drag these directly into a Word document or an Outlook email.

Lazur helps you cut through the administrative work so you can focus on the data. When you are deep in an Excel spreadsheet, you can hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about a formula or a chart feature. Lazur answers out loud, so you do not have to break your focus.

faq.question: Is there free software for energy analysis on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. The U.S. Department of Energy provides tools like MEASUR and VERIFI that are compatible with macOS and help with modeling and visualizing energy usage.

faq.question: How much time should I spend on energy data?
faq.answer: While there is no fixed rule, aim to spend your time on analysis rather than data entry. If you spend more than 30 percent of your time on entry, look for ways to automate your data imports using Power Query in Excel.
